A Step Harder, Not a Step Too Far: The Benefits and Limits of Curriculum Difficulty Progression in GRPO

Ronghan Li Affiliation: College of Artificial Intelligence, Dalian Maritime University, Dalian, 116026, Liaoning, China    Fei Chen Email: chenf@dlmu.edu.cn Affiliation: Information Science and Technology College, Dalian Maritime University, Dalian, 116026, Liaoning, China    Mingyu Lu Affiliation: College of Artificial Intelligence, Dalian Maritime University, Dalian, 116026, Liaoning, China
Abstract

Curriculum learning typically organizes training samples from easy to hard. In GRPO, medium-difficulty samples are attractive for online selection because they are more likely to yield informative group-relative learning signals, and prioritizing them can improve training efficiency. However, it remains unclear whether persistently selecting such samples also leads to the strongest final model performance, or whether training can benefit from progressing toward harder samples. Meanwhile, sample difficulty changes as the policy evolves, so fixed difficulty estimates can become misaligned with the current policy. We therefore re-estimate sample difficulty under the current policy and, inspired by the easy-to-hard principle of curriculum learning, design and evaluate a staged curriculum that progressively shifts the active difficulty band toward harder samples. Experiments on GSM8K show that persistent medium-difficulty selection does not achieve the strongest observed performance. Across three random seeds, progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band improves test accuracy to 0.6591 ± 0.0077, compared with 0.6449 ± 0.0024 for the fixed-medium curriculum. However, further progression to a harder difficulty band reduces accuracy to 0.6405 ± 0.0053. These results show that staged difficulty progression can outperform persistent medium-difficulty selection, but its benefit is non-monotonic. Effective GRPO curricula can therefore benefit from progressing beyond medium difficulty, while avoiding excessive progression toward overly difficult samples.

keywords
reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, group relative policy optimization, difficulty dynamics, curriculum learning

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides a direct way to improve reasoning models when outputs can be checked by explicit correctness rules. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) constructs policy updates from multiple responses to the same problem and does not require a separately trained value model Shao et al. (2024). Under binary correctness rewards, problems whose responses are nearly all correct or nearly all incorrect tend to produce low within-group reward variance and thus weak group-relative learning signals Xu et al. (2026). In contrast, prompts whose sampled responses differ in correctness provide nonzero reward variance for group-relative advantage estimation and can therefore yield more informative learning signals Le et al. (2026).

This property raises important questions for curriculum learning in GRPO. Classical curriculum learning typically organizes training samples from easy to hard according to estimated difficulty Bengio et al. (2009). In GRPO, however, two practical questions arise: whether difficulty estimates computed before training remain aligned with the evolving policy, and whether progressively increasing curriculum difficulty continues to provide useful learning signals. Because difficulty is relative to the current policy, the same problem may move between easy, medium, and hard difficulty bands as training proceeds. Moreover, a lower success rate does not necessarily correspond to a more informative optimization signal. Consequently, a curriculum constructed from initial difficulty can become temporally misaligned with the current policy. This motivates estimating sample difficulty online under the current policy, so that training decisions reflect the model’s current state rather than stale initial estimates. However, online difficulty estimation alone does not determine which difficulty band should be used as the policy evolves.

Figure 1 summarizes the motivation of this work. In GRPO, intermediate-solvability problems are attractive for online selection because they are more likely to generate mixed correct and incorrect responses and therefore informative group-relative signals. At the same time, difficulty may change as the policy evolves, motivating our investigation of both stale precomputed difficulty estimates and curriculum scheduling across difficulty bands.

Recent work has shown that adaptive curricula and online data selection can improve RLVR data efficiency by using reward statistics, estimated success rates, uncertainty, gradient information, or learnability signals Li et al. (2026); Bae et al. (2026); Sun et al. (2025); Gao et al. (2026); Tan et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026). In GRPO, samples with intermediate success rates are particularly relevant because they are more likely to produce groups containing both correct and incorrect responses, thereby yielding nonzero group-relative learning signals Xu et al. (2026); Le et al. (2026). This raises a further question: is continually selecting such medium-difficulty samples sufficient to maximize final model performance, or can the model benefit from progressing toward harder samples as its policy evolves? If such progression is beneficial, it remains unclear whether the benefit persists as curriculum difficulty continues to increase.

We address these questions through a sequence of curriculum experiments. First, we track the same 1,495 GSM8K training samples throughout a continuous GRPO run to characterize how sample difficulty evolves with the policy. Second, we test whether a static curriculum constructed from initial difficulty becomes misaligned with the current policy. Third, we introduce a fixed-medium curriculum that keeps the active difficulty band fixed at B3B_{3} while samples are reselected online according to the current policy. This setting tests whether continuously selecting samples from an informative medium-difficulty band is sufficient for maximizing final performance. Finally, we evaluate a staged curriculum in which the active difficulty band progresses from easier to harder bands according to the empirical success rate under the current policy. Across three random seeds, the staged curriculum achieves higher test performance at the moderately harder B4B_{4} band than the fixed-medium curriculum. However, further progression into the harder B5B_{5} band consistently reduces test performance. Together, these experiments suggest that medium-difficulty samples provide informative learning signals but are not sufficient by themselves to maximize final model capability. Progression to a moderately harder difficulty band can improve performance, whereas further increases in curriculum difficulty are not monotonically beneficial. Detailed metric definitions, additional training trajectories, and performance on the fixed diagnostic subsets used for checkpoint selection and stage transitions are provided in the appendices.

Figure 2 provides a visual comparison of the training paradigms considered in this study, highlighting the differences between static difficulty ordering, online sample selection, and staged difficulty progression.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Policy-dependent difficulty dynamics. We systematically characterize how sample difficulty changes during GRPO training and show that individual samples exhibit substantial and non-monotonic difficulty changes. We further observe that relatively stable global difficulty rankings can coexist with substantial turnover within specific difficulty bands, highlighting the limitations of relying on fixed difficulty estimates throughout training.

  • •

    Staged difficulty progression. We design and evaluate a staged curriculum that re-estimates sample difficulty under the current policy and progressively shifts the active difficulty band toward harder samples. Experiments across multiple random seeds show that persistent medium-difficulty selection does not achieve the strongest observed performance, while progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band provides additional gains. However, further progression to harder samples reduces performance, revealing a non-monotonic benefit of increasing curriculum difficulty.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on GRPO and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, dynamic data selection, and curriculum learning with model-dependent difficulty. Section 3 introduces the problem formulation and empirical framework, including policy-dependent sample difficulty and the curriculum settings considered in this work. Section 4 describes the experimental setup for difficulty tracking, static curriculum training, the fixed-medium curriculum, and the staged curriculum. Section 5 presents the empirical results on difficulty dynamics, the misalignment of precomputed difficulty, and performance under different curriculum conditions. Section 6 discusses the implications of the results, the relationship between online sample selection and difficulty progression, as well as the limitations and future directions of this study. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper by summarizing the main findings and their implications for difficulty-aware GRPO training.

2 Related Work

2.1 GRPO and RLVR

RLVR has become a major approach for improving reasoning with rule-based or otherwise verifiable rewards. DeepSeekMath introduced GRPO for mathematical reasoning, and subsequent work extended verification-based reinforcement learning to broader reasoning tasks and formal theorem proving Shao et al. (2024); Guo et al. (2025); Xin et al. (2025). Compared with PPO-based approaches that rely on an additional value model, GRPO constructs relative advantages from multiple sampled responses within the same prompt, thereby reducing reliance on explicit value estimation. Recent studies have further investigated GRPO and related reinforcement learning frameworks from the perspectives of sampling strategy, objective design, and optimization stability Yu et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025); Zheng et al. (2025).

In contrast to these algorithm-level improvements, our work focuses on the interaction between the evolving policy and training samples. Since GRPO derives learning signals from relative rewards within response groups, the usefulness of a problem is closely related to its current solvability under the current policy. However, existing GRPO studies mainly focus on optimization objectives and training stability, while the evolution of individual-sample difficulty with the policy has been less systematically characterized.

2.2 Dynamic Data Selection

Dynamic data selection aims to improve training efficiency by identifying samples that are more valuable given the current model state. Offline selection methods estimate data value using reward trajectories, influence estimation, or multi-factor scoring Li et al. (2025); Tan et al. (2025); Tang et al. (2026). In contrast, online selection methods adapt sample choices during optimization according to model-dependent signals, such as reward variance, predicted success probability, Bayesian uncertainty, transition dynamics, or gradient-related information Bae et al. (2026); Sun et al. (2025); Qu et al. (2026); Mao et al. (2026); Shen et al. (2026); Zhao et al. (2025). Other approaches, including PCL and CurES, further exploit intermediate success rates or gradient-efficient sampling strategies to improve training efficiency Gao et al. (2026); Zeng et al. (2026).

These studies motivate treating the utility of training samples as model-dependent rather than fixed. In particular, prioritizing samples with intermediate success rates provides a natural strategy for GRPO, since such samples are more likely to produce mixed correct and incorrect responses and therefore informative group-relative learning signals Le et al. (2026); Xu et al. (2026). Existing online selection methods already adapt sample choices according to the current model state. However, it remains unclear whether continuously selecting samples with intermediate solvability, even when sample difficulty is re-estimated online, is sufficient to maximize final model performance. Our work complements these studies by systematically characterizing how the difficulty of the same samples evolves with the policy and by examining the sufficiency of persistent selection of intermediate-solvability samples as the policy evolves.

2.3 Curriculum Learning with Model-Dependent Difficulty

Curriculum learning traditionally organizes training data according to estimated difficulty, following the principle of gradually increasing task complexity Bengio et al. (2009). Recent reasoning-oriented studies have incorporated curriculum strategies into reinforcement learning. E2H Reasoner explicitly organizes tasks in an easy-to-hard order Parashar et al. (2026), while Re-Schedule constructs curricula according to reasoning complexity rather than final-answer accuracy Wang et al. (2026). Other approaches, such as AdaRFT and AdaCuRL, further adjust training difficulty according to the evolving model state Shi et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026).

These difficulty-aware curriculum approaches suggest that organizing training according to model-dependent difficulty can improve training efficiency by providing samples with appropriate learning challenges. However, traditional easy-to-hard curriculum learning is built on the intuition that models benefit from being exposed to increasingly complex examples as their capabilities improve Bengio et al. (2009). This assumption may not always hold in GRPO, where optimization depends on relative rewards among sampled responses. Extremely easy problems may provide limited learning signals due to low reward variance, while extremely difficult problems may also provide limited informative comparisons when most responses are incorrect Xu et al. (2026); Le et al. (2026).

Therefore, beyond estimating sample difficulty under the current policy, an important open question in GRPO curriculum learning is whether moving toward harder difficulty bands continues to provide benefits as the policy evolves. In particular, it remains unclear whether the gains from moving to harder difficulty bands persist as curriculum difficulty continues to increase. Our work investigates this issue by characterizing how difficulty evolves with the policy and evaluating a staged easy-to-hard curriculum across increasingly difficult bands. This allows us to examine whether progressively increasing curriculum difficulty remains beneficial, rather than assuming a monotonic benefit from moving to harder difficulty bands.

3 Problem Formulation and Empirical Framework

Tables 1 and 2 summarize the main notation used throughout this paper.

3.1 Difficulty Under the Current Policy

Let πθt\pi_{\theta_{t}} denote the policy at training state tt. For a problem xx, we define its solvability under the current policy as

pt(x)=Pry∼πθt(⋅|x)[V(x,y)=1],p_{t}(x)=\Pr_{y\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|x)}[V(x,y)=1], (1)

where V⁡(x,y)∈{0,1}V(x,y)\in\{0,1\} is the correctness verifier. The corresponding true difficulty is defined as dt​(x)=1−pt​(x)d_{t}(x)=1-p_{t}(x). With GG sampled responses, we estimate solvability as

Pt​(x)=1G​∑g=1Grt,g​(x),d^t​(x)=1−Pt​(x).P_{t}(x)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}r_{t,g}(x),\qquad\widehat{d}_{t}(x)=1-P_{t}(x). (2)

Since the true solvability pt​(x)p_{t}(x) cannot be computed exactly in practice, we use the empirical success rate Pt​(x)P_{t}(x) and the corresponding estimated difficulty d^t​(x)\hat{d}_{t}(x) for all analyses.

3.2 Difficulty Dynamics

Let 𝒯={t0,t1,…,tK}\mathcal{T}=\{t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{K}\} denote the ordered sequence of checkpoints used for difficulty tracking.

We quantify the variation in empirical success rate for each problem over training using its training-period span

Ri=maxt∈𝒯⁡Pt​(xi)−mint∈𝒯⁡Pt​(xi).R_{i}=\max_{t\in\mathcal{T}}P_{t}(x_{i})-\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}P_{t}(x_{i}). (3)

We also measure the maximum absolute deviation from the initial empirical success rate as

Di,init=maxt∈𝒯⁡|Pt​(xi)−P0​(xi)|.D_{i,\mathrm{init}}=\max_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left|P_{t}(x_{i})-P_{0}(x_{i})\right|. (4)

To identify non-monotonic changes, we examine checkpoint-to-checkpoint differences

Δi,k=Ptk​(xi)−Ptk−1​(xi).\Delta_{i,k}=P_{t_{k}}(x_{i})-P_{t_{k-1}}(x_{i}). (5)

After discarding changes with |Δi,k|<δ|\Delta_{i,k}|<\delta, we count a direction reversal whenever two consecutive retained changes have opposite signs. Here, δ\delta denotes the minimum-change threshold used to suppress small fluctuations caused by finite sampling. Since each empirical success-rate estimate is based on G=32G=32 sampled responses, we set δ=0.125\delta=0.125 as the primary threshold, corresponding to four increments of 1/321/32 in the empirical success rate. Sensitivity analyses with alternative thresholds (δ=0.0625\delta=0.0625 and δ=0.25\delta=0.25) are reported in Appendix 9. We additionally examine global rank correlation and local membership changes in predefined success-rate intervals. Full definitions of retention, inflow, outflow, Jaccard similarity, mismatch, total variation, extra round-trip variation, and re-entry are given in Appendix 8.

3.3 Evaluation of Static Difficulty and Curriculum Scheduling

We examine two related questions that arise because difficulty depends on the current policy. First, we test whether curricula constructed from initial difficulty estimates become misaligned with the current policy as training proceeds. Specifically, we construct a static curriculum by estimating sample difficulty under the initial policy and fixing the resulting difficulty ordering throughout training. This setting allows us to examine whether the initial difficulty estimates remain aligned with difficulty under the current policy.

Second, we study how curriculum difficulty should be scheduled once sample difficulty is re-estimated online under the current policy. In particular, we ask whether persistently using a medium-difficulty band is sufficient to maximize final performance and whether progressing to harder difficulty bands continues to provide benefits as curriculum difficulty increases. We use the term difficulty band to denote a predefined range of policy-dependent sample difficulty used for curriculum selection. Each difficulty band BsB_{s} is operationalized by a corresponding success-rate interval [ls,us][l_{s},u_{s}]. At curriculum stage ss, BsB_{s} is referred to as the active difficulty band. A sample contributes to the policy loss only when its estimated solvability falls within the success-rate interval associated with the active difficulty band:

at(x)=𝕀[Pt(x)∈Bs].a_{t}(x)=\mathbb{I}[P_{t}(x)\in B_{s}]. (6)

Under the fixed-medium curriculum, the active difficulty band remains fixed at B3B_{3} while eligible samples are reselected online as the policy evolves. Under the staged curriculum, the active difficulty band progresses toward bands associated with lower success rates and therefore greater difficulty. Comparing these curricula allows us to examine whether online sample reselection is sufficient when the difficulty band remains fixed and how performance changes as the curriculum progresses to harder difficulty bands.

This gating mechanism is used only to define the experimental conditions. An effective update is an optimizer step in which at least one sample satisfies the gate and a parameter update actually occurs.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Model and Training Configuration

We use GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct Yang et al. (2024) and LoRA fine-tuning Hu et al. (2022). Due to different computational requirements, we use different numbers of sampled responses for difficulty estimation and online optimization. Specifically, we use G=32G=32 responses per problem for offline difficulty analysis and G=8G=8 responses per problem during curriculum experiments. The main training runs use a batch size of 8, a gradient accumulation factor of 1, a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, a temperature of 0.7, top-pp of 0.85, and a maximum generation length of 1,024 tokens. Answer correctness is used as the primary verifiable reward. An auxiliary length reward with a fixed weight of 0.2 and a preferred response-length range of 60–650 tokens is also used, but it is not used to compute Pt​(x)P_{t}(x) or make gating decisions. The official GSM8K test set is used only for generalization evaluation.

4.2 Difficulty Tracking and Static Curriculum

Before training, all 7,473 GSM8K training problems are evaluated with 32 generations each to obtain their initial solvability estimates. We first perform a reference GRPO run using the standard GRPO objective without difficulty-based filtering or curriculum scheduling. During this training process, checkpoints are saved at {0,10,20,30,40,50,100,250,500,1000,1500,2000,4000,7473}\{0,10,20,30,40,50,100,250,500,1000,1500,2000,4000,7473\}.

For performance comparison, we independently run the standard GRPO baseline with the same three random seeds used in the curriculum experiments. Each run is trained for one complete pass over the 7,473 GSM8K training problems. We retrospectively report the best observed test accuracy along each completed training trajectory; these test values are used only for post-hoc performance comparison and do not affect training, early stopping, or parameter updates.

A fixed stratified observation set of 1,495 problems (20% of the training set) is constructed by proportional sampling based on the initial solvability distribution P0​(x)P_{0}(x), preserving the original difficulty distribution of the full training set. At each checkpoint, the observation set is reevaluated with 32 generations under the corresponding policy to obtain updated solvability estimates Pt​(x)P_{t}(x) and characterize difficulty changes over training.

The static easy-to-hard curriculum first estimates the difficulty of training samples under the initial policy and ranks all training problems in descending order based on their initial solvability P0​(x)P_{0}(x), where a higher solvability score indicates an easier sample. This ordering is fixed throughout training without further difficulty re-estimation. To assess how the fixed difficulty ordering becomes misaligned with the evolving policy, the next 500 samples in the training order are reevaluated at steps 1000, 2500, 3500, 4500, 5500, and 6500.

The static curriculum is independently repeated with three random seeds. For the multi-seed static curriculum comparison, we retrospectively report the best observed test accuracy along each completed training trajectory; these test values are used only for post-hoc performance comparison and do not affect training, early stopping, or parameter updates. Its best observed test performance is reported in Sec. 5.3, while the complete difficulty-misalignment statistics for the static curriculum and multi-seed results are provided in Appendix 11.

4.3 Fixed-Medium and Staged Curricula

The staged curriculum progressively moves the active difficulty band through B1→B2→B3→B4→B5B_{1}\rightarrow B_{2}\rightarrow B_{3}\rightarrow B_{4}\rightarrow B_{5}. Based on the initial solvability estimate P0​(x)P_{0}(x), five fixed diagnostic subsets are constructed sequentially for B1B_{1} through B5B_{5}, with 128 problems assigned to each subset. To ensure that the diagnostic subsets are mutually exclusive despite the overlapping success-rate intervals, any problem already assigned to an earlier diagnostic subset is excluded from subsequent subset construction. These diagnostic subsets are used only to monitor the staged curriculum and are excluded from training, leaving 6,833 training candidates.

Every 50 effective updates, the diagnostic subset corresponding to the current curriculum stage is evaluated, with eight responses generated for each problem. Stage transitions follow a fixed patience-based rule applied to the diagnostic trajectory. A later checkpoint is treated as a new best only when its diagnostic accuracy exceeds the current best by more than the empirical noise tolerance of 0.0107. Once a new best checkpoint is established, training continues for two additional diagnostic evaluations after 50 and 100 additional effective updates, respectively. If neither subsequent evaluation improves upon the current best by more than 0.0107, the stage is considered to have reached a plateau. Neither fluctuations within the noise tolerance nor performance decreases are treated as meaningful improvements.

If a new best is observed during the patience window, the 100-update patience criterion is restarted from that checkpoint. The best checkpoint retained for the current stage is then used to initialize training in the next difficulty band. The GSM8K test set is used only for generalization evaluation and is never involved in stage-transition or checkpoint-selection decisions. The full diagnostic trajectories, noise analysis, and selected checkpoints are reported in Appendix 10.

Motivated by online data-selection strategies that prioritize samples with intermediate success rates, we introduce a fixed-medium curriculum for complementary comparison. Such samples are attractive in GRPO because they are more likely to produce mixed correct and incorrect responses and therefore informative group-relative learning signals. However, informative learning signals do not necessarily translate into the strongest final model performance. We therefore ask whether repeatedly selecting the medium-difficulty band is sufficient to maximize final model performance.

In the fixed-medium curriculum, the active difficulty band remains fixed at B3=[0.375,0.625]B_{3}=[0.375,0.625] throughout optimization, while samples are reselected online according to the evolving policy. This curriculum preserves online difficulty estimation and online sample selection while keeping the active difficulty band fixed. Comparing fixed-medium curriculum with the staged curriculum allows us to examine whether progressing to harder difficulty bands can provide additional benefits beyond repeatedly selecting samples currently in the medium-difficulty band.

Because the fixed-medium curriculum has no stage-transition criterion, we report the best observed test accuracy along each trajectory for comparison; these test values are not used to guide training or parameter updates. This retrospective best-observed value is used only for post-hoc comparison with the staged curriculum and does not affect training or staged checkpoint selection.

All multi-seed experiments use the same three random seeds. For reporting convenience, we refer to them as Seed 1, Seed 2, and Seed 3, corresponding to random seeds 42, 2026, and 100, respectively. For each staged run, stage transitions and checkpoint selection follow the same diagnostic-based criterion described above. We compare performance at the selected B4B_{4} checkpoint with performance after 100 additional effective updates in B5B_{5}. Multi-seed results are reported as mean ±\pm standard deviation.

5 Results

5.1 State Dependence and Non-Monotonicity of Difficulty

The 1,495 tracked problems become easier on average, with the mean empirical success rate increasing from 0.6554 to 0.7975. At the same time, individual trajectories vary substantially. The mean training-period span is 0.2770, and 54.72% of samples have a training-period span of at least 0.25. At the final checkpoint, the mean absolute change from the initial empirical success rate P0P_{0} is 0.1583, with 50.50% of samples changing by at least 0.125 relative to their initial values.

Non-monotonic changes are common. With δ=0.125\delta=0.125, 53.38% of samples exhibit at least one direction reversal, and 36.79% exhibit at least two. The prevalence of direction reversals is threshold-dependent, rising to 87.02% for δ=0.0625\delta=0.0625 and falling to 4.95% for δ=0.25\delta=0.25. Across the five difficulty bands, roughly 81–84% of samples that leave their initial band later re-enter it. Detailed sensitivity and re-entry statistics are reported in Appendix 9.

Figure 3 summarizes both the population-level magnitude and non-monotonicity of changes in empirical solvability, while also providing representative problem-level trajectories.

5.2 Global Ordering Persistence and Local Band-Membership Change

Global rank ordering remains largely preserved even when local band membership changes substantially. The Spearman rank correlation between P0P_{0} and the final PTP_{T} remains 0.8092. In contrast, only 20.74% of samples initially in the medium-difficulty band B3=[0.375,0.625]B_{3}=[0.375,0.625] remain there at the final checkpoint, while 65.00% of the samples in B3B_{3} at the final checkpoint entered from outside the initial band. These results show that a relatively stable global difficulty ranking does not imply stable membership within a specific difficulty band. In other words, rank correlation can remain high even when the set of samples occupying a given difficulty band changes substantially. Full rank and membership tables are given in Appendix 9. An additional visualization of the relationship between the initial and final rank percentiles is provided in Appendix 9.1, where the concentration near the diagonal offers a more direct view of the preserved global ordering.

Figure 4 visualizes this contrast directly: global rank consistency remains relatively high throughout training, whereas membership in the medium-difficulty band undergoes substantial turnover.

5.3 Precomputed Difficulty Misalignment in Static Curriculum Training

The static curriculum provides evidence of difficulty misalignment over training. At step 5500, the next 500 scheduled problems have a planned mean success rate of 0.3986 under the initial policy but a current mean success rate of 0.5573, with a mean absolute deviation of 0.1863. Similar mismatches appear at earlier checkpoints, although their magnitudes are not monotonically related to test accuracy. We therefore interpret this analysis as evidence that precomputed difficulty estimates can become temporally misaligned with the evolving policy, rather than as evidence that such misalignment alone causes performance degradation. The complete table is reported in Appendix 11.

Despite this misalignment, static curriculum training remains a competitive baseline. Across Seeds 1, 2, and 3, the best observed test accuracies are 0.6535, 0.6497, and 0.6535, respectively, corresponding to 0.6522±0.00220.6522\pm 0.0022. Therefore, the observed difficulty mismatch should not be interpreted as implying that a precomputed easy-to-hard curriculum becomes ineffective. Rather, these results indicate that the difficulty estimates underlying the fixed schedule can become outdated even when the resulting curriculum still achieves strong performance.

5.4 Performance Across Difficulty Bands

The two online curriculum conditions highlight two complementary effects. First, in one detailed experimental run, persistently selecting the medium-difficulty band does not yield the strongest observed performance. The fixed-medium curriculum reaches a best observed test accuracy of 0.6459 while keeping the difficulty band at B3=[0.375,0.625]B_{3}=[0.375,0.625], whereas the staged curriculum reaches 0.6558 at the selected B4B_{4} checkpoint. This comparison suggests that repeatedly selecting samples currently in the medium-difficulty band, despite their informative group-relative learning signals, is not sufficient to achieve the strongest observed performance; moving to a moderately harder difficulty band can provide additional gains.

Second, the benefit of progression does not persist as curriculum difficulty continues to increase. After the staged run transitions from B4B_{4} to the harder B5B_{5} band, test accuracy decreases from 0.6558 to 0.6391 after 50 additional effective updates and further to 0.6353 after 100 additional effective updates. The corresponding B5B_{5} diagnostic accuracy also decreases from 0.5215 at entry to 0.4971 and 0.4512. The concurrent decline in both diagnostic and test performance suggests that this deterioration is not merely a transient fluctuation in test accuracy.

Taken together, this detailed run indicates that the performance benefit of moving to harder difficulty bands is non-monotonic: remaining in the medium-difficulty band can leave additional gains unrealized, whereas further progression into the harder difficulty band can offset the gains obtained from moderate progression.

Although the staged and fixed-medium curricula follow different training trajectories, the observed performance gap suggests that persistently selecting the medium-difficulty band is insufficient to achieve the strongest observed test performance. Sec. 5.5 examines the consistency of this pattern across random seeds.

Figure 5(a) visualizes the Seed 1 trajectory, including the improvement observed during B4B_{4} and the subsequent decline after progression into B5B_{5}.

5.5 Robustness Across Random Seeds

The qualitative pattern described in Sec. 5.4 is observed across all three random seeds. As shown in Table 6, at the selected B4B_{4} checkpoints, the staged curriculum achieves test accuracies of 0.6558, 0.6535, and 0.6679 for Seeds 1, 2, and 3, respectively, corresponding to 0.6591±0.00770.6591\pm 0.0077. In comparison, the best observed accuracies along the fixed-medium trajectories are 0.6459, 0.6422, and 0.6467, yielding 0.6449±0.00240.6449\pm 0.0024. Performance at the selected B4B_{4} checkpoints exceeds the best observed fixed-medium performance in all three runs by 0.99, 1.13, and 2.12 percentage points, respectively.

For the standard GRPO baseline, the best observed test accuracies are 0.6459, 0.6414, and 0.6459 for Seeds 1, 2, and 3, respectively, corresponding to 0.6444±0.00260.6444\pm 0.0026. Performance at the selected B4B_{4} checkpoints of the staged curriculum is higher than the best observed standard GRPO performance in all three runs, by 0.99, 1.21, and 2.20 percentage points, respectively.

Figure 5(b) summarizes the corresponding multi-seed comparison across the main training conditions. The static curriculum provides an additional strong baseline, with best observed test accuracies of 0.6535, 0.6497, and 0.6535 across the three runs, corresponding to 0.6522±0.00220.6522\pm 0.0022. Nevertheless, performance at the selected B4B_{4} checkpoints is higher than that of the static curriculum in all three runs by 0.23, 0.38, and 1.44 percentage points, respectively.

Further progression into B5B_{5} shows the opposite pattern across all three seeds. After 100 additional effective updates in B5B_{5}, test accuracies decrease to 0.6353, 0.6404, and 0.6458 for Seeds 1, 2, and 3, respectively, corresponding to 0.6405±0.00530.6405\pm 0.0053. Relative to the selected B4B_{4} checkpoints, these results represent decreases of 2.05, 1.31, and 2.21 percentage points, respectively.

Taken together, the multi-seed results support the same conclusion as the detailed analysis in Sec. 5.4: persistent selection of the medium-difficulty band is insufficient to attain the strongest observed test performance, while test performance at the selected B4B_{4} checkpoints is consistently higher than the best observed results from standard GRPO, the fixed-medium curriculum, and the static curriculum across all three seeds. However, further progression into B5B_{5} consistently reduces performance. These results are consistent with a non-monotonic relationship between scheduled difficulty and performance, rather than a monotonic benefit from continually increasing difficulty.

6 Discussion

Our results provide two main insights into difficulty-aware GRPO training. First, sample difficulty is policy-dependent and can change substantially and non-monotonically as training proceeds. Consequently, difficulty estimates obtained under the initial policy may become misaligned with the current policy, even when the global difficulty ranking remains relatively stable. The competitive performance of the static curriculum, however, shows that such misalignment does not by itself make a precomputed curriculum ineffective. Rather, these observations motivate re-estimating sample difficulty under the current policy when sample selection depends on current solvability.

More importantly, our experiments distinguish informative learning signals from final model performance. Medium-difficulty samples are attractive for online selection because they are more likely to produce mixed correct and incorrect responses and therefore informative group-relative learning signals. However, the fixed-medium curriculum shows that persistently selecting such samples does not yield the strongest observed performance. The staged curriculum instead benefits from progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band, whereas further progression to a harder difficulty band consistently reduces performance across random seeds. This pattern suggests a non-monotonic relationship between curriculum difficulty and model performance: remaining at medium difficulty can leave additional gains unrealized, while increasing difficulty too far can offset the gains obtained from moderate progression.

These findings suggest that online sample selection and difficulty progression should be treated as two related but distinct components of difficulty-aware GRPO training. Online difficulty estimation determines which samples currently belong to a given difficulty band, whereas difficulty progression determines which difficulty band is used at different stages of training. Our results indicate that combining online re-estimation with staged difficulty progression can improve performance beyond persistent medium-difficulty selection, but progression toward harder samples should not be continued indefinitely. Effective curriculum design therefore requires not only identifying informative samples under the current policy, but also controlling how far the curriculum progresses in difficulty.

Several limitations remain. Our experiments focus on a single model family and the GSM8K benchmark, so the generality of the observed difficulty dynamics and curriculum pattern should be evaluated across broader models and reasoning tasks. Online solvability is estimated from only eight sampled responses, which introduces noise into difficulty estimation and sample selection. In addition, the staged curriculum relies on fixed diagnostic subsets and a predefined transition criterion, and it uses a smaller training candidate pool than the other conditions. Comparisons involving the staged curriculum should therefore be interpreted as complete-procedure comparisons rather than strict single-factor evaluations. Future work should examine these findings in broader settings, improve the accuracy and efficiency of online difficulty estimation, and develop more general adaptive mechanisms for determining when curriculum difficulty should increase and when further progression should stop.

7 Conclusion

We investigated how sample difficulty changes during GRPO training and whether persistently selecting medium-difficulty samples is sufficient for achieving strong final performance. The results show that sample difficulty changes with the evolving policy, supporting the use of current-policy difficulty estimates for online sample selection.

More importantly, the curriculum experiments reveal that persistent medium-difficulty selection does not achieve the strongest observed performance. Across three random seeds, progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band provides additional gains, whereas further progression to a harder difficulty band consistently reduces performance. These findings show that the benefit of increasing curriculum difficulty is non-monotonic. Overall, effective GRPO curriculum design should combine online sample selection with staged difficulty progression, moving beyond persistent medium-difficulty selection while avoiding excessive progression toward overly difficult samples.

8 Detailed Difficulty-Dynamics Metrics

This appendix gives the detailed metrics used to characterize local difficulty-band changes and non-monotonic trajectories.

For a difficulty band BB with associated success-rate interval [l,u][l,u], let

St​(B)={xi∣Pt​(xi)∈[l,u]}.S_{t}(B)=\{x_{i}\mid P_{t}(x_{i})\in[l,u]\}. (7)

We characterize changes in band membership using the following complementary metrics.

Retentiont​(B)\displaystyle\mathrm{Retention}_{t}(B) =|S0​(B)∩St​(B)||S0​(B)|,\displaystyle=\frac{|S_{0}(B)\cap S_{t}(B)|}{|S_{0}(B)|}, (8)
Outflowt​(B)\displaystyle\mathrm{Outflow}_{t}(B) =1−Retentiont​(B),\displaystyle=1-\mathrm{Retention}_{t}(B), (9)
Inflowt​(B)\displaystyle\mathrm{Inflow}_{t}(B) =|St​(B)∖S0​(B)||St​(B)|,\displaystyle=\frac{|S_{t}(B)\setminus S_{0}(B)|}{|S_{t}(B)|}, (10)
Jaccardt​(B)\displaystyle\mathrm{Jaccard}_{t}(B) =|S0​(B)∩St​(B)||S0​(B)∪St​(B)|,\displaystyle=\frac{|S_{0}(B)\cap S_{t}(B)|}{|S_{0}(B)\cup S_{t}(B)|}, (11)
Mismatcht​(B)\displaystyle\mathrm{Mismatch}_{t}(B) =|S0​(B)​△​St​(B)|N.\displaystyle=\frac{|S_{0}(B)\triangle S_{t}(B)|}{N}. (12)

Here NN is the number of samples in the fixed observation set and △\triangle denotes symmetric difference.

Retention measures the fraction of samples initially belonging to band BB that remain in the same band at training state tt, while Outflow measures the complementary fraction that has left the band. Inflow measures the fraction of current band members that did not belong to BB initially, capturing replacement by newly entering samples. Jaccard similarity quantifies the overlap between the initial and current band memberships. Mismatch measures the size of their symmetric difference relative to the full observation set of N samples, reflecting the overall extent of membership disagreement. Together, these metrics characterize sample persistence, departure, entry, set overlap, and overall membership change.

To distinguish one-directional movement from repeated back-and-forth changes, we use

T​Vi=∑k=1K|Ptk​(xi)−Ptk−1​(xi)|,TV_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}|P_{t_{k}}(x_{i})-P_{t_{k-1}}(x_{i})|, (13)

and define the extra round-trip variation as

Ei=T​Vi−Ri.E_{i}=TV_{i}-R_{i}. (14)

Here, Ei=0E_{i}=0 for a monotonic trajectory, whereas Ei>0E_{i}>0 indicates variation beyond the observed success-rate span caused by back-and-forth changes. To define re-entry, let

Ii,k(B)=𝟏{Ptk(xi)∈B}.I_{i,k}(B)=\mathbf{1}\{P_{t_{k}}(x_{i})\in B\}. (15)

indicate whether sample xix_{i} belongs to band BB at checkpoint tkt_{k}. A sample is counted as having ever left band BB if there exist checkpoints ta<tbt_{a}<t_{b} such that Ii,a​(B)=1I_{i,a}(B)=1 and Ii,b​(B)=0I_{i,b}(B)=0. Among these samples, a sample is counted as re-entering band BB if there exists a later checkpoint tc>tbt_{c}>t_{b} such that Ii,c​(B)=1I_{i,c}(B)=1. We define the re-entry rate as

ReEntry(B)=|{xi:∃a<b<c,Ii,a(B)=1,Ii,b(B)=0,Ii,c(B)=1}||{xi:∃a<b,Ii,a(B)=1,Ii,b(B)=0}|.\mathrm{ReEntry}(B)=\frac{\left|\left\{x_{i}:\exists\,a<b<c,\;I_{i,a}(B)=1,\;I_{i,b}(B)=0,\;I_{i,c}(B)=1\right\}\right|}{\left|\left\{x_{i}:\exists\,a<b,\;I_{i,a}(B)=1,\;I_{i,b}(B)=0\right\}\right|}. (16)

Thus, the denominator consists only of samples that have been observed in band BB and subsequently left it at least once, rather than all samples that ever belonged to the band or the full observation set.

10 Diagnostic Trajectories and Stage Selection

Five fixed diagnostic subsets of 128 problems are constructed for the staged curriculum, one for each difficulty band B1B_{1}–B5B_{5}. The subsets are constructed sequentially from B1B_{1} through B5B_{5}, and any problem already assigned to an earlier diagnostic subset is excluded from subsequent subset construction. These subsets are used only to monitor training progress and are excluded from the training pool, so they do not contribute to parameter updates. During each curriculum stage, the diagnostic subset corresponding to the active difficulty band is evaluated every 50 effective updates, with eight responses generated for each problem.

To estimate the scale of diagnostic evaluation noise, the same model and diagnostic subset are reevaluated ten times using different sampling seeds. The resulting accuracies have a mean of 0.5226, a standard deviation of 0.0042, a minimum of 0.5156, and a maximum of 0.5283. The empirical 95th percentile of pairwise absolute accuracy differences is approximately 0.0107. We use this value as an empirical noise tolerance when determining whether a later diagnostic evaluation represents a meaningful improvement over the current best checkpoint.

Stage transitions follow a fixed patience-based criterion. Within each stage, a later checkpoint is treated as a new best checkpoint only when its diagnostic accuracy exceeds the current best by more than the empirical noise tolerance of 0.0107. Once a new best checkpoint is established, training continues for two additional diagnostic evaluations after 50 and 100 additional effective updates, respectively. If neither subsequent evaluation improves upon the current best by more than 0.0107, the stage is considered to have reached a plateau. The retained best checkpoint is then used to initialize training in the next difficulty band. If a new best checkpoint is observed during this patience window, the 100-update patience criterion is restarted from that checkpoint. When multiple checkpoints lie within the same high-performing plateau and their diagnostic-accuracy differences remain within the empirical noise tolerance, the earlier checkpoint is retained.

Table 12 summarizes the checkpoints selected for the three random seeds.

Figure J1 provides a visual summary of the diagnostic trajectories underlying the stage-selection decisions reported in Tables C6–C9.

The complete diagnostic trajectories used for stage selection are reported below. Bold values indicate the checkpoints retained for initialization of the subsequent stage.

No post-entry B5B_{5} checkpoint is selected for any of the three seeds. For Seed 1, the B5B_{5} diagnostic accuracy decreases from 0.5215 at entry to 0.4971 after 50 effective updates and 0.4512 after 100 effective updates. For Seed 2, the corresponding diagnostic accuracies are 0.5127, 0.5086, and 0.4521, while for Seed 3 they are 0.5745, 0.5713, and 0.5273. Thus, no run shows a diagnostic improvement after progression into B5B_{5}, and the selected B4B_{4} checkpoint remains the final selected checkpoint for each seed.
